description: Hi! I’m Paras, a B.Sc. Computer Science student interested in Data Science, AI/ML, NLP, and Web Development. For NASA Space Apps 2026, I’m exploring the “Flame in Freefall” challenge to build an AI-powered solution using NASA’s microgravity combustion data. Looking for teammates skilled in AI/ML, data analysis, visualization, software, UI/UX, space science, research, or presentation. 🚀
summary:
NovaForge is an interactive dashboard built for NASA Space Apps’ “Flame in Freefall” challenge. NASA’s microgravity combustion research is valuable for spaceflight fire safety, but the findings can be difficult to locate, compare, and interpret. NovaForge brings those investigations into one place so researchers, students, and engineers can explore what was studied and see where information is missing.

Users can browse and compare investigations, explore fire-safety topics such as materials, smoke and dust detection, and suppression, and view rankings for environments including the ISS, Moon bases, Mars bases, spacecraft, rovers, and spacesuits. The dashboard keeps experimental evidence separate from inferred relevance and distinguishes oxygen concentration, total pressure, and calculated oxygen partial pressure. Source links and data-type labels help users trace values; unavailable data is shown as missing rather than guessed.

The site also includes NASA-related Earth applications, data gaps, methodology, exports, and a grounded assistant that can abstain when the available records do not support an answer. It is an educational research tool, not a certified safety system or NASA endorsement.
details:
NovaForge’s Flame in Freefall is an interactive dashboard that helps researchers and students explore NASA’s microgravity combustion research for future spacecraft, space stations, lunar and Mars habitats, pressurized rovers, and spacesuits. It organizes NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations so users can search by fuel, conditions, hardware, and safety topic; compare investigations; explore NASA-linked safety technologies; and export the loaded dataset.

The dashboard currently includes 26 investigation summaries and a PSI-22 experimental table with 21 source rows. These are a query snapshot, not the full PSI repository. The SI assistant retrieves relevant records, cites its sources, and should say when available evidence cannot answer a question. Its default demo mode uses cached answers.

Our creative approach is to make decades of difficult-to-navigate research easier to compare by environment while keeping recorded evidence separate from inferred relevance. For oxygen scenarios, the dashboard treats oxygen concentration, total pressure, and calculated oxygen partial pressure as distinct quantities.

We built the project with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Node.js. It uses NASA PSI data, Zod for schema validation, Fuse.js for search, TanStack Table for data views, Recharts for visualizations, and Vitest and Playwright for testing.

We prioritized source traceability, honest representation of missing data, clear separation of measurements from calculations and inferences, and careful communication of safety limits. The intended impact is to support research and education—not to certify materials or replace professional spacecraft safety analysis.
